statement: In adolescents and young adults who use cannabis frequently or heavily, compared with people of similar age who use little or no cannabis, cannabis use is associated with slightly lower scores on memory and thinking tests in studies that did not give cannabis to participants (the hours after a single dose given in a laboratory are covered by the answer on how long impairment lasts). In a meta-analysis of 69 cross-sectional samples published 1973 to 2017 (2,152 people who used cannabis, mean age 20.6, and 6,575 comparison participants with minimal use; Scott et al., 2018; AMSTAR 2 confidence critically low), the average difference in mostly raw test scores, not adjusted for other drug use, education or ability before use, was about a quarter of a standard deviation (d −0.25, 95% CI −0.32 to −0.17): learning −0.33, executive shifting −0.30, delayed memory −0.26, speed of processing −0.26, inhibition −0.25, working memory −0.22 and attention −0.21, with no clear difference on verbal or language (−0.14, −0.27 to 0.001), visuospatial (−0.04, −0.16 to 0.08) or motor tests (−0.02, −0.22 to 0.18). Results varied widely between studies (editors' approximate 95% prediction interval −0.77 to +0.28); 22 of the 69 studies required no abstinence before testing or did not say; samples of people seeking treatment differed more (−0.43, −0.62 to −0.24; 12 studies; uncorrected P = .04); and small studies reported larger differences: allowing for missing small studies shrank the estimate of a simpler model from −0.21 to −0.13. The difference was smaller in studies that required a longer time without cannabis before testing: −0.08 (−0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies) where more than 72 hours was required, against −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22) where 72 hours or less was required or none was stated; this compares studies, not the same people over time (see the answer on stopping). A systematic review of 2004-2015 studies (Broyd et al., 2016; critically low; nothing pooled) rated the evidence of poorer verbal learning and memory and attention in people who use cannabis regularly as strong and largely consistent (20 and 14 studies), and the evidence for working memory, planning-type executive functions, inhibition and decision making as mixed (a narrative review of the same year calls the findings for working memory, attention and impulsivity mixed; Curran et al., 2016, second-hand); more than half of its studies did not report IQ or education, and its authors suggest that links with how often people use may reflect lingering effects of recent use. Two cohorts that measured IQ in childhood add to this: in a British twin cohort, the 84 of 1,989 18-year-olds with cannabis dependence performed worse than the others on 4 of 6 executive-function scores, 2 after allowing for IQ at 12, but did not differ from their co-twins in 57 pairs in which only one twin was dependent (Meier et al., 2018); in a New Zealand birth cohort, 9 of 16 test scores at 38 (executive function, memory, processing speed, and two WAIS-IV index scores for perceptual reasoning and verbal comprehension) were lower the more of five interviews from 18 to 38 at which people had met criteria for dependence, after allowing for childhood IQ and sex, without correction for testing many scores, and these tests had not been given in childhood (Meier et al., 2012). The two reviews share primary studies and are counted once. None of these comparisons can show that cannabis caused the differences. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: On average, young people who use cannabis often score a little lower on tests of learning, memory, attention and planning than people of the same age who use little or none: about a quarter of a standard deviation, which is a small difference. Tests of language, of shapes and space, and of movement showed no clear gap. The gap was smaller in studies that asked people to go more than 3 days without cannabis before the test, bigger in people seeking treatment, and small studies may have made it look bigger. These studies tested people after they had started using, so they cannot show that cannabis caused the gap; in one twin study, the gap on thinking tests at 18 was smaller and no longer clear when each twin was compared with their co-twin.
population: Adolescents and young adults (sample mean ages 26 or younger; mean age about 21) who use cannabis frequently or heavily, most with frequent use or a cannabis use disorder, in cross-sectional studies; members of two population cohorts (New Zealand, born 1972-73; England and Wales, twins born 1994-95)
exposure: Frequent, heavy or problematic cannabis use as each study defined it (amount, potency and route mostly not recorded); in the cohorts, DSM cannabis dependence in the past year at 18 (British twins) or at up to five interviews from 18 to 38 (New Zealand)
comparator: People of similar age with minimal or no cannabis use, as each study defined them; in the twin analysis, the co-twin without dependence
outcome: Scores on standardized memory, attention, processing-speed, executive, verbal, visuospatial and motor tests in studies that did not give cannabis, as group differences in standard-deviation units; abstinence before testing ranged from none to about 3 months
magnitude: Scott et al. 2018 (69 samples; 2,152 against 6,575; raw-score Hedges-corrected d, negative = lower in the cannabis groups): overall −0.247 (95% CI −0.32 to −0.17), between-study variance 0.070 (P < .001; editors' approximate prediction interval −0.77 to +0.28); learning −0.33 (−0.42 to −0.24); executive abstraction/shifting −0.30 (−0.40 to −0.20); speed −0.26 (−0.38 to −0.15); delayed memory −0.26 (−0.35 to −0.16); inhibition −0.25 (−0.38 to −0.13); updating/working memory −0.22 (−0.31 to −0.12); attention −0.21 (−0.31 to −0.12); verbal/language −0.14 (−0.27 to 0.001); visuospatial −0.04 (−0.16 to 0.08); motor −0.02 (−0.22 to 0.18). Required abstinence more than 72 h −0.08 (−0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies, n = 928) against 72 h or less −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22; 54 studies, n = 7,799), P = .01. Treatment-seeking −0.43 (−0.62 to −0.24; 12 studies) against others −0.22 (−0.29 to −0.14), uncorrected P = .04. Small-study effects: Egger t = 4.70, P < .001; trim-and-fill in a univariate model −0.206 to −0.128. Broyd et al. 2016 (qualitative ratings, chronic use): verbal learning and memory +++ (20 studies), attention +++ (14), working memory +– (16), planning-type executive functions +– (23), inhibition +– (9), decision making +– (17), psychomotor function + (10). Meier et al. 2018 (age 18; 84 with dependence among 1,989; sex-adjusted z-scores): 4 of 6 executive scores worse (Spatial Span Forward −0.48 against 0.02), 2 of 6 after IQ at 12; 57 discordant twin pairs, no significant difference (Spatial Span Forward −0.38 against −0.18, p = .20). Meier et al. 2012 (age 38; tests without childhood baseline, adjusted for childhood IQ and sex): significant trend with waves of dependence on 9 of 16 test scores, two of them WAIS-IV index scores for perceptual reasoning and verbal comprehension; no correction for multiple testing.

evidence.locator: Abstract (AM p. 2); Figure 1, PRISMA flow diagram (AM p. 27)
evidence.extracted: Systematic review of studies published January 2004 to February 2015 on acute and chronic effects of cannabis and cannabinoids on cognitive task performance and on persistence or recovery after abstinence: 3,021 records from PubMed and 3,220 from Scopus, 356 full-text records screened, 260 excluded and 105 studies included in a qualitative synthesis, with nothing pooled (editors' arithmetic on the study card: 356 minus 260 leaves 96, so the flow does not add up).

evidence.locator: Table 1, Chronic rating column, Number of studies CHRONIC column, key and footnote
evidence.extracted: The review's ratings of the evidence for impairment in people who use cannabis regularly (chronic column, with the number of chronic studies): verbal learning and memory +++ (20 studies); attention +++ (14); attentional bias +++ (7); working memory +– (16); other memory functions +– (8); psychomotor function + (10); planning, reasoning, interference control and problem solving +– (23); inhibition +– (9); verbal fluency +– (6); decision making +– (17); time estimation – (1). Key: +++ strong and largely consistent evidence for impairment; + weak, based on few studies; +– mixed; – little or no evidence. The footnote calls the ratings a qualitative interpretation, subjectively weighed on the number and quality (design, sample size) of studies and reached by consensus of the review's authors.

evidence.locator: Results › Memory › Verbal learning and memory, paragraph (begins AM p. 4, continues on p. 5); Results › Attention, paragraph (AM p. 5)
evidence.extracted: Impaired verbal learning and memory continues to be consistently observed in people who use cannabis regularly, in adolescents (refs 45–47) and young adults (refs 48–52, but not refs 53 and 54), and in one study even in occasional use (ref. 55); poorer performance has been associated with frequency, quantity, duration and age of onset of use, and long-term use appears more affected than short-term use (refs 60, 61). Attention: many studies report impairment in adolescents and adults who use cannabis and in people who had stopped for up to several weeks, while others found no difference between people abstinent after past use and controls on broader attention measures; the authors suggest that attentional impairment may reflect residual effects that fade as cannabinoids are cleared from the body.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (AM p. 8); Discussion › Specificity to cannabis and potential confounds, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (AM p. 9)
evidence.extracted: The authors note that in studies of people who use cannabis regularly, associations with frequency of use are more likely to reflect residual effects of acute or subchronic intoxication, associations with dose residual or cumulative effects, and associations with duration more persistent alterations; about 75% of the studies had mostly male samples. More than 50% of the studies did not report IQ or years of education, a substantial number did not control for functioning before use, and many failed to report or account for alcohol, tobacco and other drug use; the impairing effects of chronic use mostly held after controlling for other substance use, but not in all studies.

evidence.locator: Long-term effects, 1st paragraph (begins p. 296, continues on p. 297) and 2nd paragraph (p. 297)
evidence.extracted: Second-hand (narrative review): studies of long-term effects rely mainly on retrospective self-report by people who chose to use cannabis; long-term memory impairments have been reported mainly in frequent, heavy use, and confounders (ability before use, alcohol and other drugs, type of cannabis, age at onset, and mental health problems including depression and problem cannabis use) make cause and effect hard to establish. Case-control studies are called inconsistent; the most consistent finding is poorer encoding of new episodic memories, with persisting deficits in some studies over the first few days of abstinence but little evidence of deficits at 28 days (as summarised from a review, ref. 25); working memory, attention and impulsivity findings are mixed; one study found no difference in decision making or risk taking against controls matched for mental-health confounds, although in that study poorer decision-making accuracy went with more symptoms of problem cannabis use (ref. 35).

evidence.locator: Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Results › Associations between Cannabis Dependence and Executive Functions, 1st paragraph; Table 4
evidence.extracted: Of the 1,989 twins analysed, 84 met DSM-IV criteria for past-year cannabis dependence at 18. Executive functions were measured only at 18 (CANTAB; sex-adjusted z-scores; 83 to 84 people with dependence and 1,895 to 1,902 without, some scores missing): the full sample with dependence scored lower on Rapid Visual Processing A prime (−0.22 against 0.02, p = .024), Spatial Working Memory strategy (0.21 against −0.01, p = .017; higher is worse), Spatial Span Forward (−0.48 against 0.02, p < .001) and Reversed (−0.33 against 0.01, p < .001), not on false alarms or errors; after adjusting for IQ at 12, only Spatial Span Forward (−0.35 against 0.01) and Reversed (−0.20 against 0.01, p = .030). In 57 twin pairs discordant for dependence no test differed (p = .20 to .72; Spatial Span Forward −0.38 against −0.18, p = .20). There is no baseline before use for these tests.

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional comparisons of raw scores, not adjusted for ability before use, education or other drug use, with no study-level appraisal in either review (AMSTAR 2 critically low: cards sc_scott_2018, sc_broyd_2016); more than half of the studies in one review did not report IQ or education. The cohort findings carry their own risks (sc_meier_2012, ROBINS-E high for confounding; sc_meier_2018, some concerns).

inconsistency.note: Wide spread between studies (between-study variance 0.070, P < .001; approximate prediction interval −0.77 to +0.28); findings for working memory, executive functions and decision making are mixed. Part of the spread is explained by abstinence before testing and treatment seeking.

indirectness.note: Second-hand (METHODS §6.3): the primary studies inside both reviews were not read, and Broyd et al.'s ratings are its authors' consensus. Most samples used frequently or had a use disorder and were young, which the claim states; the estimates do not describe occasional use or older adults.

imprecision.note: The pooled interval is narrow (−0.32 to −0.17), and seven domain intervals exclude zero.

publication_bias.note: Funnel asymmetry and a significant Egger test (t = 4.70, P < .001); trim-and-fill shrank the estimate by about 38%; the search was limited to English-language peer-reviewed studies.

dose_response.note: Associations with frequency, duration and age of onset are reported by Broyd et al. but not pooled, and its authors read the frequency links as possible residual effects; Scott et al. found no moderation by age at first use. No upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Differences that predate use and other drug use would more plausibly enlarge than hide the differences; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational (cross-sectional) evidence starts low and is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness (second-hand) and publication bias, which is below the floor: very low. Rated as worded, an association in young people who use cannabis frequently, tested when not intoxicated; whether differences remain after stopping, and whether cannabis lowers IQ, are separate answers. Status replicated: the direction is the same in most of the independent primary studies in both reviews (for verbal learning and memory, Broyd et al. cite 8 studies in adolescents and young adults that found poorer scores and 2 that did not), though the size varies widely. Overlap: Scott et al. (1973 to 2017) and Broyd et al. (2004 to 2015) share primary studies (Fried et al., 2005, for example, is in both), and Dunedin is among Broyd et al.'s studies, so the reviews are counted once and not as independent replication; the British twin cohort is independent of both pools.
